title: Automatic Temporal Relation in Multi-Task Learning

problem.claim: The central challenge is exploiting shared temporal information between prediction tasks to improve model generalization and robustness.

gap.claim: Existing temporal-relation approaches use predefined and symmetric task structures that are too rigid to capture intricate temporal relations.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Automatic Temporal Relation (AutoTR), a mechanism that directly and automatically learns temporal relations from a given dataset.
The biconvex objective is addressed with alternating optimization, closed-form proximal operators for the two subproblems, and an accelerated proximal gradient method.
The authors provide an implementation source for AutoTR.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe AutoTR as a novel mechanism for automatically learning temporal relations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report preprocessing six public real-life datasets and conducting extensive experiments.
The authors report that AutoTR outperforms several baseline methods on almost all datasets across different training ratios, for overall and individual-task performance.
The authors report findings that temporal relations between tasks are asymmetrical.

narrative_sequence.summary: Temporal relations are used in multi-task learning to model evolving systems and jointly analyze multiple time points.
The key challenge is exploiting shared temporal information, while existing predefined symmetric relation structures are too rigid.
AutoTR automatically learns temporal relations, using alternating optimization, proximal-operator computation, and accelerated proximal gradients.
Experiments on six public real-life datasets are reported to show superiority over baselines and asymmetry in task relations.

source_observation.claim: Predefined symmetric temporal structures may be too rigid, and the reported task relations are asymmetrical.

interpretation.claim: Temporal dependencies should be learned flexibly and should not assume symmetry without evidence.

application.claim: For multi-task problems indexed by time, consider learning directed or otherwise adaptive task relations from data.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when learned asymmetry is preferable or how it behaves outside the reported datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six datasets, baseline identities, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not provide details of the model architecture, objective formulation, or computational costs.
The abstract does not independently verify the reported superiority or asymmetry findings.
